Habits

Nail-biting and other hard-to-break habits

Nail-biting, hair-pulling or skin-picking are usually automatic. A simple technique helps break them.

You realise you are biting your nails when you have already been at it for a while. Or that while reading you twist your hair, pick at your skin or pinch it. These are very common behaviours and are often done without noticing.

Automatic habits

Psychology calls them body-focused repetitive behaviours. They tend to appear at moments of boredom, concentration or tension, and produce a small relief or satisfaction that reinforces them. Over time they become automatic: the movement starts before we decide. At their most intense, when they cause damage or great distress, they are considered disorders, such as trichotillomania or excoriation disorder.

Habit reversal training

In 1973, Nathan Azrin and Gregory Nunn proposed habit reversal, which remains the best-supported technique. It has three main steps:

  • Awareness: note when, where and with what emotion the habit appears, and learn to spot the first signs of the movement.
  • Competing response: as soon as the urge appears, do something for a minute that prevents the movement, such as gently clenching your fist or resting your hands on your thighs.
  • Support: ask someone you trust to point it out or encourage you.

A family of habits

Nail biting belongs to a group of body-focused repetitive behaviours, along with hair pulling (trichotillomania), skin picking or biting the inside of the cheeks. They are common, often start in childhood or adolescence and tend to appear at times of boredom, tension or concentration. In their more intense forms they can cause wounds, infections and shame, and the WHO classification places them alongside obsessive-compulsive disorder.

Training awareness

An effective first step is learning to notice the habit: keeping a record of when, where and with what emotion it appears. Many people discover they do it almost without realising, for example while watching TV or reading. With that information, specific alternatives can be prepared for those moments, such as keeping something in their hands or keeping nails short and well cared for.

Other useful ideas

  • Keep your hands busy with a small object at risky moments.
  • Put up barriers: short nails, thin gloves or plasters on your fingertips.
  • Address the underlying emotion: if the habit increases with stress, work on the stress too.
If it causes wounds, infections or great embarrassment, a psychologist can help with a structured treatment.

References

  1. Azrin, N. H. y Nunn, R. G. (1973). Habit-reversal: a method of eliminating nervous habits and tics. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 11(4), 619–628.
  2. Lee, M. T., Mpavaenda, D. N. y Fineberg, N. A. (2019). Habit reversal therapy in obsessive compulsive related disorders: a systematic review. Frontiers in Psychiatry, 10, 79.
  3. Grant, J. E. y Chamberlain, S. R. (2016). Trichotillomania. American Journal of Psychiatry, 173(9), 868–874.
  4. Organización Mundial de la Salud (2019). CIE-11: Clasificación Internacional de Enfermedades, 6B25: Trastornos de comportamiento repetitivo centrado en el cuerpo.
